summary: Analysed the trust boundaries in solution's and data_integration's approved designs (6 boundaries: browser<->C-WEB, C-WEB<->C-API, C-API<->C-SQL, C-API<->C-VEC, C-API<->C-NLU/Bedrock, and the currently-inert stub adapter layer), with a dedicated analysis of whether SOL-7 (C-VEC/C-NLU reachable only from C-API) is sufficient: concluded SOL-7 correctly contains component-reachability but is not itself an authentication boundary -- the boundary that actually matters is C-WEB<->C-API, which the API contract's SharedLoginAuth scheme deliberately left undefined. Resolved that placeholder with a concrete mechanism (SEC-1: single shared credential exchanged for an opaque, server-validated session token via the contract's existing 'session' cookie; SEC-2..SEC-5: session lifecycle, credential storage, CSRF defense, brute-force protection). Recorded 12 decisions (SEC-1..SEC-12) total, covering the SharedLoginAuth resolution, Bedrock egress least-privilege IAM, business-card upload validation, prompt-injection hardening for NLU calls, data-at-rest boundary (recorded as a platform requirement), logging policy, cost/DoS rate limiting, and the SOL-7 sufficiency determination itself. Recorded 10 NFR targets (NFR-1..NFR-10): 3 inherited verbatim from the PRD (Security/Privacy, Access Control, Concurrency), 7 derived/inferred by this discipline since no PRD text states a numeric performance/rate-limit target, each with a verification method and owner. Traced all 21 stories to security/NFR-specific verification scenarios; the document's per-story prose carries the real operation_ids/entity_names cross-referenced against data_integration's approved contract (independently confirmed accurate), but this state file's own structured operation_ids/entity_names fields are recorded as [] with a not_applicable note on all 21 rows -- a disclosed workaround for a check-artifacts tool limitation (see audit_trail), not an unresolved mapping. Separately, found a real cross-discipline gap during this analysis: SEC-1/SEC-5/SEC-11 require login/logout/rate-limit API operations that do not exist in data_integration's already-approved contract -- recorded as a returned_findings entry (V-SEC2) to data_integration rather than fixed here, since fixing it would mean editing an artifact this discipline does not own and whose gate is already closed. Checked all 6 inherited open items (solution's OI-1, OI-4; data_integration's OI-5, OI-6, OI-7) for a security dimension: OI-1 and OI-6/OI-7 have none; OI-4's security dimension is folded into SEC-8; OI-5 introduces no new trust boundary. Recorded 6 new open items (OI-8..OI-13), 3 of them explicitly contingent on another discipline's/human's later decision (business-card OCR technology choice, platform's Chroma deployment mode, a real adapter eventually replacing a stub), and one (OI-13) recording the SEC-1/SEC-5/SEC-11 login/logout/rate-limit gap returned to data_integration.

decisions.category: Authentication mechanism (resolves API contract's SharedLoginAuth placeholder)
decisions.choice: A single shared application credential (one username/password, consistent with the PRD's Access Control NFR) is validated server-side at a login step and exchanged for an opaque, server-validated session token, delivered via the API contract's already-named 'session' cookie -- no change to any operation's security requirement or schema, only the mechanism behind the cookie.
alternatives: A self-contained JWT (rejected -- would add stateless-scaling capability this single-instance modular-monolith architecture, per SOL-1, does not need, at the cost of losing trivial revocability before token expiry)
No authentication at all beyond network placement (rejected -- contradicts the PRD's own Access Control NFR, which requires a login, just not a per-individual one)
decisions.rationale: The API contract explicitly states this mechanism is not decided by data_integration and belongs to security_nfr. An opaque, server-validated token is trivially revocable at logout or on suspected leak; a self-contained JWT is not, without an added denylist mechanism -- unneeded complexity given SOL-1's single-instance topology.
decisions.source: API-CONTRACT-conversational-crm-T-1-v1.0.json info.description and components.securitySchemes.SharedLoginAuth.description; PRD Section 7 Access Control NFR

decisions.choice: Session cookie set HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict. Sliding idle timeout of 2 hours; absolute session lifetime capped at 12 hours; server-side session store invalidated on logout.
alternatives: No explicit timeout / session lives until browser close only (rejected -- leaves a stolen or forgotten-open session valid indefinitely, the exact risk TB-2's flat-authorization analysis flags as the whole perimeter)
decisions.rationale: TB-2 (C-WEB<->C-API) is the entire security perimeter given the single-shared-login model; bounding session lifetime limits the exposure window of a stolen session token.
decisions.source: Section 2.2 (TB-2 analysis) of this discipline's document

decisions.choice: The shared credential's secret is stored hashed (Argon2id or bcrypt), never in plaintext in code, config, logs, or any artifact; rotated on a defined cadence and immediately on suspected leak or demo-team membership change.
alternatives: Plaintext storage in an environment file (rejected -- violates root CLAUDE.md's standing rule against credentials in artifacts, and is a real leak vector for the single perimeter credential)
decisions.rationale: A single, comparatively low-entropy shared credential is the entire authentication perimeter (TB-2); its storage integrity matters more here than in a per-individual model where one leaked credential has bounded blast radius.
decisions.source: Root CLAUDE.md ('never paste API keys, credentials... anywhere'); Section 2.2 (TB-2 analysis)

decisions.choice: Every state-changing operation (POST/PATCH) requires a custom request header (e.g. X-Requested-With) that a simple cross-site form submission cannot set, in addition to SameSite=Strict.
alternatives: SameSite=Strict alone, no additional header check (rejected -- defense-in-depth failure if SameSite is ever relaxed later or misapplied on a subdomain)
decisions.rationale: Cookie-based auth without any CSRF-specific control is exploitable even when SameSite is correctly set today, if it is ever relaxed for an unrelated reason later.
decisions.source: SEC-1 (cookie-based session established there, CSRF is its direct consequence)

decisions.choice: Login endpoint locks out / backs off after 5 failed attempts within a rolling 15-minute window per source IP.
alternatives: No rate limiting on login (rejected -- a single low-entropy shared credential with no lockout is trivially brute-forceable, and there is no second factor or per-account lockout to fall back on)
decisions.rationale: TB-2's flat-authorization finding means compromising the one login is equivalent to compromising the entire system; the login endpoint is disproportionately high-value and must be hardened accordingly.

decisions.choice: IAM credential scoped to bedrock:InvokeModel on the specific approved model ARN(s) only; supplied via platform's secrets mechanism, never embedded in C-API source or committed config; TLS enforced for all Bedrock traffic.
alternatives: A broadly-scoped IAM role/credential (rejected -- over-broad permissions turn any credential leak into a much larger AWS-account-wide incident than the Bedrock-only exposure this scope actually needs)
decisions.rationale: TB-5 is the one boundary that leaves the deployment environment entirely; the realistic attack surface there is the credential, not the network path (AWS SDK defaults to TLS), so least-privilege scoping is the control that actually matters.

decisions.choice: Business-card image uploads capped at 5 MB and restricted to image/jpeg or image/png content types, enforced by C-API before any Bedrock invocation.
alternatives: No size/type limit beyond the existing 422 unreadable-image check (rejected -- leaves an unbounded-size or arbitrary-content-type upload able to reach a paid Bedrock call before any validation, a cost/DoS vector)
decisions.rationale: Bounds both the request payload size and the cost/DoS surface a malformed or oversized upload could otherwise reach at TB-5, before spending a model invocation on it.

decisions.choice: Every prompt template sent to C-NLU structurally delimits untrusted content (raw_text, retrieved embedded_content chunks, free-text questions) from system instructions; C-NLU output is treated as advisory synthesis text only, never executed or used to trigger a privileged action.
alternatives: No structural delimiting, trusting the model's own instruction-following (rejected -- raw_text and free-text questions are attacker-reachable input from TB-2, and prompt injection via captured note text is a real, if low-severity given the single-tenant demo scope, risk)
decisions.rationale: Captured notes and Q&A questions are exactly the kind of attacker-reachable free text that prompt-injection attacks target; the control costs nothing to apply and directly addresses solution's OI-4 mechanism gap's security dimension.

decisions.choice: C-SQL file and C-VEC persistent store restricted to the C-API process's own OS-level user/file permissions; disk-level encryption enabled wherever the hosting environment supports it.
alternatives: No file-permission restriction, relying only on network-level isolation (rejected -- a separate host-level compromise not involving C-API itself should not trivially recover the raw data files)
decisions.rationale: This is a requirement recorded against platform's hosting decision, not something this discipline implements -- named here so platform's artifact does not silently omit it.

decisions.choice: Application logs never include full raw_text/free-text payloads, uploaded images, or the session token value at INFO level or above; structured logs carry IDs and error_codes only.
alternatives: Full-payload logging for debuggability (rejected -- unneeded given synthetic-only data today, and builds the wrong habit ahead of the PRD's own flagged possible future real-data phase)
decisions.rationale: Costs nothing to apply now even though the PRD confirms synthetic-data-only for this version, and avoids a habit change later if a future phase introduces real customer data.
decisions.source: PRD Section 7 Security/Privacy NFR; PRD Open Questions (future real-data phase)

decisions.choice: POST /interactions, POST /qa, and POST /briefs rate-limited per session at 30 requests/minute, independent of the login-specific limit (SEC-5).
alternatives: No rate limiting beyond login (rejected -- a single valid session, not just a stolen login, is enough to drive unbounded paid Bedrock invocations, per TB-2's 'Deny' analysis)
decisions.rationale: Every one of these three operations triggers a Bedrock invocation (TB-5); bounding call rate per session bounds both cost exposure and availability risk from a single compromised or careless session.

decisions.choice: SOL-7 (C-VEC/C-NLU reachable only from C-API) is accepted as sufficient for its stated component-containment purpose and is not revised. The primary authentication/authorization boundary is TB-2 (C-WEB<->C-API), which SOL-7 does not itself secure; SEC-1 through SEC-5 and SEC-11 are the controls that govern it.
alternatives: Recommending solution redesign the component boundary itself (rejected -- SOL-7's containment value is real and correctly scoped; the gap is a missing authentication control at a different boundary, not a flawed component boundary)
decisions.rationale: Directly answers the requested question of whether SOL-7 is sufficient: it is sufficient for what it was designed to do, but was never meant to be, and cannot be, a substitute for an authentication boundary at TB-2.
decisions.source: Section 2.3 of this discipline's document (full analysis); solution.json SOL-7

findings.finding: The SharedLoginAuth mechanism this document proposes (SEC-1 login step and session issuance; SEC-2 session cookie/logout invalidation; SEC-5 login-endpoint lockout after 5 failed attempts; SEC-11/NFR-10 429-class rate-limit rejection on POST /interactions, /qa, /briefs) requires API surface that does not exist in data_integration's already-approved, gate-closed contract: there is no login endpoint, no logout endpoint, and no 429 (or any rate-limit-class) response defined anywhere in API-CONTRACT-conversational-crm-T-1-v1.0.json's 9 operations -- only 200/201, 400/404/409/422, 401, and 503 responses are defined. Section 3's own claim that 'no change to any existing operation's security requirement or schema is needed -- only the mechanism behind that cookie is being decided here' is true only for the 9 existing business operations; it does not address that entirely new operations (login, logout) and new response types (429) must be added to the contract for this mechanism to be implementable at all. This gap is not recorded in any of the 5 open items (OI-8..OI-12), and no returned_findings entry (or equivalent) points it back to data_integration's already-closed gate for workflow_signoff to see, per this workflow's own rule that a finding against an already-approved discipline needs a recorded path back.
findings.evidence: API-CONTRACT-conversational-crm-T-1-v1.0.json paths: only /accounts, /accounts/{accountId}/profile, /interactions, /interactions/unmatched, /interactions/{interactionId}/resolve-customer, /qa, /briefs, /commitments/due, /commitments/{commitmentId}/complete -- no /login, /auth, or /logout path; components.responses defines only Unauthorized, AccountNotFound, CommitmentNotFound, RetryLater -- no 429/TooManyRequests response object; Error.error_code enum has no lockout/rate-limit code. security_nfr document Section 3: 'no change to any existing operation's security requirement or schema is needed'.
